**Chemistry**

**36**

Any atom can be divided into electrons, protons and neutrons. This chapter will focus on various models of the atom, fundamental particles of atom, configuration of the electrons etc.

**By the end of the chapter, we will be able to**

* write symbols of elements from their English and Latin names
* describe the characteristics of fundamental and stable particles
* describe atomic number, mass number and relative atomic mass
* calculate the relative molecular mass from the relative atomic mass
* calculate the number of electrons, protons and neutrons of an atom
* explain the uses of isotopes
* describe the Rutherford and Bohr models of atom's structure
* explain whether the Rutherford or the Bohr model is more acceptable
* arrange electrons of atoms in orbits and different sub-orbits

**## 2.5 Burning of a Candle and the Three States of Wax**

A candle is made of wax, which is a mixture of various hydrocarbons. When a candle is lit, the wax melts and vaporizes, forming a gas that rises to the surface of the flame. The wax then solidifies and falls back down to the wick, where it is heated again and vaporized. This process continues until the candle is burned out.

**## 2.6 Melting and Boiling**

Melting and boiling are two important physical changes that occur in matter. Melting is the transition from a solid to a liquid, while boiling is the transition from a liquid to a gas. Both processes involve the absorption of energy by the substance.

**## 2.7 Sublimation**

Sublimation is the transition from a solid to a gas without going through the liquid phase. This process occurs when the intermolecular forces between the molecules of a substance are weak enough that they can escape into the air as a gas.

**## 2.8 Deposition**

Deposition is the transition from a gas to a solid without going through the liquid phase. This process occurs when the intermolecular forces between the molecules of a substance are strong enough that they can condense into a solid.

**## 2.9 Condensation**

Condensation is the transition from a gas to a liquid. This process occurs when the intermolecular forces between the molecules of a substance are strong enough that they can come together and form a liquid.

**## 2.10 Evaporation**

Evaporation is the transition from a liquid to a gas. This process occurs when the intermolecular forces between the molecules of a substance are weak enough that they can escape into the air as a gas.

**## 2.11 Distillation**

Distillation is a method of separating a mixture of liquids based on their boiling points. It involves heating the mixture and collecting the vapor, which is then condensed and collected as a separate liquid.

**## 2.12 Chromatography**

Chromatography is a method of separating a mixture of substances based on their interactions with a stationary phase and a mobile phase. It involves passing the mixture through a column or paper, which separates the substances based on their properties.

**## 2.13 Electrophoresis**

Electrophoresis is a method of separating a mixture of substances based on their charge and size. It involves passing the mixture through an electric field, which separates the substances based on their properties.

**## 2.14 Spectroscopy**

Spectroscopy is a method of analyzing the interaction between matter and electromagnetic radiation. It involves measuring the absorption or emission of radiation by a substance, which provides information about its composition and structure.

**## 2.15 X-Ray Crystallography**

X-ray crystallography is a method of determining the structure of a crystal by analyzing the diffraction pattern of X-rays scattered by the crystal. It involves measuring the intensity of the scattered X-rays, which provides information about the arrangement of atoms within the crystal.

**## 2.16 Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Spectroscopy**

NMR spectroscopy is a method of analyzing the interaction between matter and magnetic fields. It involves measuring the absorption or emission of radiation by a substance, which provides information about its composition and structure.

**## 2.17 Mass Spectrometry**

Mass spectrometry is a method of analyzing the mass-to-charge ratio of ions. It involves measuring the mass-to-charge ratio of ions, which provides information about their composition and structure.

**## 2.18 Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS)**

GC-MS is a method of analyzing the composition of a mixture of substances. It involves separating the substances based on their boiling points and then measuring their mass-to-charge ratio.

**## 2.19 Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS)**

LC-MS is a method of analyzing the composition of a mixture of substances. It involves separating the substances based on their interactions with a stationary phase and a mobile phase, and then measuring their mass-to-charge ratio.

**## 2.20 Tandem Mass Spectrometry (MS/MS)**

MS/MS is a method of analyzing the composition of a mixture of substances. It involves measuring the mass-to-charge ratio of ions and then fragmenting them to produce smaller ions, which are then measured again.

**## 2.21 Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS)**

ICP-MS is a method of analyzing the composition of a mixture of substances. It involves measuring the mass-to-charge ratio of ions produced by an inductively coupled plasma.

**## 2.22 Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry (TOF-MS)**

TOF-MS is a method of analyzing the composition of a mixture of substances. It involves measuring the time it takes for ions to travel through a magnetic field, which provides information about their mass-to-charge ratio.

**## 2.23 Quadrupole Mass Spectrometry (QMS)**

QMS is a method of analyzing the composition of a mixture of substances. It involves measuring the mass-to-charge ratio of ions by using a quadrupole filter to select ions of a specific mass-to-charge ratio.
